Senses.PreferredTarget: Bian He, presenter of the uncut jade
Senses.Explanation: Bian He is the pre-Chan jade-bearer whom the corpus invokes through the uncut-jade story. The name occurs 78 times in 47 allowlisted texts. The Book of Serenity retells the defining event: Bian He found an uncut stone in a valley of Mount Jing, offered it to King Li of Chu, was told it was stone, and had one foot cut off. Chan interviews compress the story into answers such as “white jade without flaw; Bian He has his foot cut off” (白玉無瑕，卞和刖足). A student explicitly adopts the role by saying, “I bring the uncut jade to the master and ask the master to carve and polish it”; when the master refuses it as beam material, the student says, “then Bian He has nowhere to emerge” (卞和無出身處). Yuanwu’s verse names the repeated offering and its cost: “laughable, Bian He presents the jade three times; even if honored, both feet are cut off” (卞和三獻玉，縱榮刖却一雙足). Another verse draws its own comparison: “Mount Jing’s fine jade—why discern it? … Bian He had knowledge; the king of Chu rejected him” (卞和有智楚王嫌). Zen therefore deploys Bian He as the named bearer of unrecognized jade in answers, student self-comparison, verses, and case commentary. These records, not a general literary biography, define the entry.
Senses.Note: Finder, presenter, amputated man, and student-adopted role all refer to the same allusion figure. Differences in whether a passage stresses jade, recognition, repeated presentation, or punishment are deployments, not separate senses.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, 'not mind, not buddha' (非心非佛). The corpus records it as a saying, an answer, a question, and the second member of the sequence beginning with 'this mind is this buddha' (即心即佛). In the Mazu exchange, a monk asks why Mazu says 'this mind is this buddha'; Mazu answers, 'to stop a small child crying' (為止小兒啼). Asked, 'What about when the crying stops?' (啼止時如何), he replies, 'not mind, not buddha' (非心非佛). Funiu Zizai explicitly names the pair: 'This mind is this buddha is a sentence seeking medicine where there is no illness; not mind, not buddha is a sentence countering medicine and illness' (即心即佛是無病求藥句非心非佛是藥病對治句). Other records set it beside the expanded expression 'not mind, not buddha, not a thing' (不是心不是佛不是物), ask 'What is not mind, not buddha?' (如何是非心非佛), or treat it as a question answered with another recorded saying—for example, Heshan answers, 'Heshan knows how to beat the drum' (禾山解打鼓). Damei Fachang's case preserves an explicit contrast: told that Mazu now says 'not mind, not buddha,' Damei answers that he still keeps 'this mind is this buddha.'
Senses.Note: The exact phrase occurs 727 times in 213 allowlisted texts; the question 'What is not mind, not buddha?' (如何是非心非佛) occurs 47 times in 35 texts. Searches found one 'as for not mind, not buddha' form (非心非佛者) and one 'call it not mind, not buddha' form (喚作非心非佛), but neither yielded a fuller literal definition than the Funiu classification. The paired and expanded forms are preserved as related recorded expressions, not merged into one interchangeable formula. The term is corpus-wide even though its best-known early occurrence belongs to Mazu's exchange.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancient Worthies' Recorded Sayings (古尊宿語錄), transmitted Mazu exchange. Mazu says 'not mind, not buddha' after the question about the child's crying stopping; because this is transmitted narrative, no direct master link is assigned.
